name: Parsi
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.source_named: Retired ISO code merged into Gujarati [guj]; only Glottolog's most extensive description is Palsetia 2001 (ethnography/a wordlist or less), no phonological description

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2022. Change Request 2022-009: merge [prp] Parsi into [guj] Gujarati (adopted 2023-01-20). SIL International.
sources.note: Nothing. p. 2: Parsis 'speak a variety of Gujarati with some Iranian lexical material not otherwise present in Gujarati (Gajendragadkar 1974, Modi 2011)'; the [prp] entry is 'spurious'. Names the two descriptive works: Gajendragadkar 1974 and Modi 2011.

sources.citation: Shih, Shu-hao 2018 (Rutgers diss.), Shih & de Lacy 2019 (CatJL), Bowers 2019, Shih 2016 - Gujarati stress sources already held by the project
sources.note: a full-text search for stress/accent: no mention in any of them; they describe standard Gujarati stress only.

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. 1908. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. IX (Indo-Aryan, Central Group), Part II: Specimens of the Rajasthani and Gujarati. Calcutta: Superintendent of Government Printing.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Gujarati introduction (the scanned text): 'The Parsis and Musalmans are usually credited with special dialects, but in pronunciation and inflexion these generally follow the colloquial Gujarati of their neighbours.. The Gujarati of Parsis and Musalmans mainly differs from the ordinary colloquial language of the uneducated in its vocabulary'; also (line 38096) Parsi Gujarati 'often exhibits the change of cerebral letters to dentals'. No Parsi specimen; no accent statement for Gujarati in the volume.

sources.citation: Tisdall, William St. Clair. 1892. A simplified grammar of the Gujarati language. London: Trübner.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the book (only 'emphasis' in grammatical senses). pp. 15-16: Parsi Gujarati is one of 'three main varieties', differing in Persian/Arabic/Urdu vocabulary and a grammar 'in a very unfixed and irregular condition'; grammar 'practically one and the same' across Hindu/Parsi/Muslim speakers. p. 25: dahado 'in Parsi-Gujarati pronounced daro'.
Nothing; retired bookkeeping entry 'Merged into [guj] Gujarati', no bibliography listed.
Parsi dialect noted as 'highly distinctive.. considerable lexical influence by Avestan'; no word-stress information; cites Tisdall 1892 for the three varieties.

sources.citation: Modi, Bharati. 2011. Parsi Gujarati: Vanishing dialect, vanishing culture (Languages of the World/Materials 483). Munich: LINCOM Europa. 152 pp.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Modern LINCOM sketch of the dialect; LW/M volumes normally open with a phonology section that may include a stress note. Cited by ISO CR 2022-009 as a primary source.

sources.citation: Doctor, Raimond. 2004. A grammar of Gujarati. Munich: LINCOM Europa.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained

sources.note: Lists Parsi Gujarati among minority dialects and has a Gujarati stress section ('Stress, although predictable, exhibits extremely complicated patterns'); may note dialectal differences.

sources.citation: [Author not visible]. 2025. Sociolinguistic variation and codeswitching between Parsi Gujarati and English. Journal of Asian Linguistic Anthropology 7(4).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists at the publisher (DOI recorded); open or paywalled, not checked; only the abstract or an excerpt is openly accessible
sources.note: Only recent linguistic study of Parsi Gujarati found; sociolinguistic, unlikely to state stress, but its background section may cite any newer phonological description.

sources.citation: de Lacy, Paul. 2006. Markedness: Reduction and preservation in phonology. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press (Gujarati stress chapter).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Google Books snippet shows the Gujarati stress discussion explicitly labels certain exceptional forms as Parsi-Gujarati, i.e. the one place in the stress literature that says something about Parsi Gujarati stress. The same material is in de Lacy 2002, The formal expression of markedness (UMass diss., ROA-542), but roa.rutgers.edu was unreachable on 2026-09-17.

sources.citation: Gajendragadkar, S. N. 1974. Parsi-Gujarati: A descriptive analysis. Bombay: University of Bombay. 226 pp.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: The only full descriptive analysis of the dialect (phonology, grammar, comparison with Standard Gujarati pp. 97-99, texts pp. 101-226). Snippet shows §1.1 sets stress/intonation aside; the book must be opened to confirm whether any section states stress placement or explicitly declines to treat it.

sources.citation: Cardona, George. 1965. A Gujarati reference grammar. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, HathiTrust search-only; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 3254.50.30); the linked copy is not accessible
sources.note: The standard Gujarati stress description that de Lacy 2006 and Shih 2018 build on; since [prp] is merged into Gujarati (guja1252), this is the statement that would cover Parsi Gujarati if the catalog treats it under Gujarati.

sources.citation: Palsetia, Jesse S. 2001. The Parsis of India: Preservation of identity in Bombay. Leiden: Brill. (Glottolog's only reference for pars1251)
sources.tag: not read: abstract or record only
sources.note: Ethnography; quoted by ISO CR 2022-009 (pp. 13-14) only for the Parsis having 'fashioned their own Gujarati dialect that utilized Persianized forms and vocabulary'. Not consulted (paywalled), no phonology expected.

sources.note: No phonological or prosodic study of Parsi Gujarati surfaced beyond Gajendragadkar 1974 and Modi 2011. Only other linguistic hit: a 2025 sociolinguistic codeswitching article (JALA, DOI 10.47298/jala.v7-i4-a4), landing page behind a captcha.
